body:
We make Kiron, so weigh this accordingly. Everything here about Ladder comes from its website, pricing page and App Store listing, and recent App Store reviews, checked November 15, 2026. Everything about Kiron describes version 1.2.

Most people looking for a Ladder alternative have hit one of two walls: the price or the phone. Ladder starts at $179.99 a year, and there's no Android app. Here's what Kiron (that's us) offers instead, and who Ladder is still worth it for.

Ladder or Kiron? The quick verdict

  • Choose Kiron if you want a proven plan with the thinking done for you, for {{kiron:price-annual}} against Ladder's $179.99. Pick a program for your goal, and Kiron lays out your workouts, works out your weights and tells you why.
  • On Android? Ladder has no Android app, only a version that runs in a web browser. Kiron has full apps for {{kiron:cell-platforms}}.
  • Stay with Ladder if you want a coach: a real person who writes your team's week, a video and a voice that talk you through every set, teammates to train with, and an Apple Watch app.

Bottom line: Ladder sells coaching; Kiron sells the plan. If you'll press play and follow a coach most days, Ladder earns its price. For most people, we think a good plan is what matters, and Kiron delivers one for less than a third of the price, on {{kiron:cell-platforms}}.

What Kiron is

Kiron is a workout app for {{kiron:cell-platforms}} that plans your training around a program you choose. There are three ways to start:

  • Pick one of {{kiron:program-count}} ready-made programs by goal, days a week, equipment and experience.
  • Answer a few questions, and Kiron builds a program for you.
  • Bring a plan you already have. Paste it from ChatGPT, a coach or a website, or snap a photo, and Kiron turns it into a program on your calendar.

After that, the planning is Kiron's job:

  • Your next workout is ready when you open the app, whether you train on set days or whenever you make it to the gym.
  • Every lift starts with a suggested weight and a short note on where it came from, then a quick "How did it feel?" check.
  • Weights go up as you get stronger, and Kiron says why: "You hit every set, so we added 5 lb."
  • Variety that keeps your main lifts. Smaller exercises can change from week to week while the big lifts stay put, so you can watch them climb.
  • Travel gyms. Save a hotel or second gym with its equipment, and Kiron swaps in exercises that fit.
  • Runs and race plans on the same calendar as your lifting, from a first 5K to a marathon.
  • Recovery that counts your other workouts, like runs and rides that other apps save to Apple Health or Health Connect.
  • {{kiron:price-annual}}, less than a third of Ladder's yearly price.

Ladder sorts you onto a team by style. In Kiron you pick the style, from programs like Kettlebell Strength, HIIT Conditioning, Push / Pull / Legs, Glute Builder, Run + Lift and Joint-Friendly Strength. Many follow formats lifters and runners have used for decades, so you start from a proven structure.

Ladder's coach, or Kiron's plan

Ladder's pitch is a coach. After a short quiz, you join one of 23 coach-led "teams," each with its own style, from bodybuilding and kettlebells to HIIT and Pilates with strength. Every Sunday the coach releases the team's week. You press play, and each workout runs with a video of every movement, the coach's voice in your ear and a timer for every set. Coach and teammates talk in a group chat.

Kiron has no coach. It meets the same need, knowing exactly what to do when you walk into the gym, with a plan made for you:

  • Your plan, not the team's. Ladder's site says its programs are designed for a whole team, not for each member. A Kiron program runs on your schedule, with your equipment and your weights.
  • Weights with a reason. When Kiron picks a weight, a short note on the exercise says why. It might come from your recent sessions (a little lighter after time away) or from a related lift: "You did 100 lb × 8 on EZ Bar Curl, so we started Hammer Curl at 35 lb per hand." New to a lift? You start light. After a set, Kiron asks "How did 35 lb feel?" (too easy, just right or too hard) and adjusts the sets still to come.
  • Training when life allows. Run a program on fixed days, and Kiron can move missed workouts forward for you. Or choose Whenever I train: no dates, the next workout waits for whenever you show up, and nothing is ever marked missed. Two workouts in a day or five in a week is fine.
  • Change your mind freely. Switch programs whenever you like, follow a running plan and a lifting plan side by side, or paste in a new plan.

In fairness, Ladder has added flexibility this year. Since an August update you can move a rest day or train twice in a day, and a late-October update lets you edit a workout before you start it. Both apps log your weights and reps, flag new personal records and work with Apple Health.

What Ladder costs, and what Kiron costs

Ladder's pricing page shows one plan, PRO, paid two ways. Monthly is $29.99, for one team you can change twice a month. Yearly is $179.99 up front (Ladder calls it $14.99 a month), with every team and unlimited changes. Twelve months of the monthly plan comes to $359.88, about the cost of two years on the yearly plan, so if you're staying, pay yearly.

The App Store also lists three higher plans: PRO+, ELITE and ELITE+, from $34.99 to $49.99 a month or $329.99 to $479.99 a year. Ladder's site says they add one-on-one coaching and form checks.

Paying monthly, Kiron is {{kiron:price-monthly}}, or {{kiron:price-monthly-yearly}} if you keep it all year, which is still less than Ladder PRO's yearly price. On the yearly plans, it's {{kiron:price-annual}} against $179.99.

Is Ladder on Android?

No. Ladder's own site says there's no Android app, and its FAQ offers a waitlist with no date. On an Android phone, the closest thing is Ladder's web version at joinladder.com/app, which covers workouts, the team chat and the training journal in a browser. Ladder calls the iPhone app the full product, and food logging, for one, is iPhone-only.

Kiron has full apps for {{kiron:cell-platforms}}.

Who should stay with Ladder

Plenty of people. Stay if:

  • You want a coach. A named person writes your team's week, new every Sunday, and answers questions in the team chat. Kiron has no coaches.
  • You like being talked through it. Ladder plays a video of each movement with the coach's voice in your ear. Kiron shows an animated demo for most exercises, with no voice.
  • Teammates keep you going. Every Ladder plan includes the team chat. Kiron has no chat or feed.
  • You train from your wrist. Ladder has an Apple Watch app. Kiron has none, and reads heart rate from Apple Health or Health Connect after a workout.
  • You want food logging in the same app. Ladder tracks calories, protein, carbs and fat at no extra cost. Kiron doesn't track food.
  • You'd pay with HSA or FSA money. Ladder's yearly PRO plan can be paid from a health savings account or flexible spending account (see below). Kiron can't.
  • You'd rather try it without payment details. Ladder's 7-day trial asks for none until it ends. Kiron has {{kiron:trial}} too, but it starts through the App Store or Google Play and renews unless you cancel.
  • You value a long track record. Ladder has more than 220,000 ratings on the US App Store, and 480 of its 500 most recent US reviews give four or five stars. Kiron is new and still small.

Ladder questions, answered

Is Ladder worth the money?

It is if you'll use the coaching: the coach's week, the follow-along videos and the team. Price comes up in 5 of its 20 recent reviews at three stars or lower; a 3-star reviewer in November wrote that "the monthly rate of 29.99 is more than the cost of a gym membership." If you mainly want a plan to follow, you'd be paying for coaching you skip.

Is there a cheaper or free app like Ladder?

Nothing free comes with Ladder's coaching, though Ladder posts a free workout of the day on its website. Boostcamp's free tier includes 99 of its 132 coach-designed programs, on iPhone and Android. Hevy's free plan logs your workouts, and its $23.99-a-year Pro plan can build a lifting program (see Hevy vs Kiron). Kiron is {{kiron:price-monthly}} or {{kiron:price-annual}}, with no free version. Our guide to workout apps for following a program sorts the rest by the job they do.

Can I cancel Ladder during the free trial?

Ladder says it takes no payment details until the 7-day trial ends, and that the monthly plan can be cancelled any time in the App Store. On an iPhone, that's Settings, your Apple Account, Subscriptions.

Can I pay for Ladder with HSA or FSA money?

Ladder says yes. Through a partner called Flex, qualifying members can pay for PRO yearly with health savings (HSA) or flexible spending (FSA) funds and a letter of medical necessity. Eligibility varies, so check with your plan administrator.

If Ladder's price or the missing Android app brought you here, and a good plan matters more to you than a coach, try Kiron. Pick a program for your goal or let Kiron build one, and your week is laid out with the weights worked out. Your Ladder history can't come along, but every first weight comes with a note. {{kiron:cta-sentence}} Get Kiron.

If you'd miss the coach in your ear and the team, Ladder is worth its price for you. Still weighing apps? See how Fitbod compares, or how to fit running and lifting into one week.
